title: Westbrook City Council — Special Meeting

fields.Location: Westbrook High School (Room 114), 125 Stroudwater St. (Hybrid via Zoom)

note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with direct quotes and timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. Summarization necessarily condenses and selects; for complete context, nuance, and anything not covered here, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)
attendance: Present: President Jennifer Munro, Vice President Michael Shaughnessy, Brian McCambridge, Anna Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham, Gary Rairdon. Absent: Victor Chau. Mayor David Morse also attended.

blocks.x: Council Messages & First Public Comment
Documentary Screening, Safe Streets Grant Question & Recreation-Area Security
Discussion Summary

Vice President Shaughnessy promoted a documentary screening ("Unless Something Goes Terribly Wrong," May 13, Performing Arts Center) about the District's wastewater treatment facility. He did so at the request of the City's Portland Water District representative. Councilor McCambridge asked why the City hadn't applied for federal Safe Streets for All grant funding. Director Dudley said the City lacked a sufficiently developed project to submit this cycle.

In public comment, Larry McWilliams followed up on a recreation-area vandalism issue (youths reportedly throwing rocks at basketball courts). Mayor Morse confirmed a mobile surveillance unit deployed about two weeks prior has had a noticeable deterrent effect. Permanent lighting is still a longer-term goal.
Key Decisions
Informational — no vote taken.
Action Items
None.
Unfinished Business
Fowl & Poultry Ordinance — Remains Tabled
Discussion Summary

City Administrator Holmes asked the Council to take no action and leave the rooster ordinance, a city law, tabled. To table an item is to set it aside to take up later. It was tabled Apr. 6 over a drafting ambiguity. This lets staff bring redrafted language to the next meeting.
Key Decisions
No action taken; item remains tabled.

None.

None.
Order 2026-42 — Land Use Ordinance — Child Care Uses (Second & Final Reading)
Found on page 43 of the packet. Public hearing held.

Action Items
None.
FY2026-2027 Budget: First Reading

Order 2026-44 (Community Center bus): authorizes $122,845 to Quality Van Sales, Inc. for a new 27/28-passenger Ford E-450 bus. It replaces a 10-year-old, ~115,000-mile bus in active use 114 of 168 open weekdays this year (58 adult trips, 14 youth programs, per Director Greg Post).
The City switched from a planned 5-year lease (~$26,170/year) to an outright purchase as more economical. This is after a $7,000 trade-in credit and $800 discount.
Passed unanimously, first reading (the first of two required votes).

Order 2026-45 (the budget itself): the bus purchase passed. So the Council first adopted a floor amendment (a change made during the meeting). It reflects the $26,170 reduction in municipal tax need. It passed 5–1 by roll call (Councilor Rairdon opposed). As amended:
Total appropriation (money approved to be spent): $106,543,473 (reduced from $106,569,643)
Municipal operating expenses: $39,021,807 (reduced from $39,047,977)
Net budget to be raised and assessed: $61,666,487 (reduced from $61,692,657)
Resulting property tax rate increase: an estimated 7.61% (reduced from 7.65% pre-amendment)

This combines a 6.30% municipal expenditure increase and 7.24% and 6.06% school increases (PreK-12 and Adult Education, in that order). It also includes a 6.62% increase in the Tax Increment Financing transfer, and a 12.37% Cumberland County assessment increase. Tax Increment Financing is tax from new development set aside for that district's projects.
(These are the Finance-Committee-refined figures; see the Apr. 6 meeting summary for the Mayor's earlier, higher preliminary estimate.)
The budget as amended passed first reading, 5–1 (Rairdon opposed), by show of hands.

“I appreciate the creativity of our departments... You have all provided thoughtful and informative presentations. And some of you have been met with hostility and accusations, and that's not fair to you... If you are over the age of 65 in this community and have lived here for more than eight years, please look at [the senior tax credit]. Being eligible for up to $1,000 will help offset the increase from this year and some of last year's.”

“As we started the budget season... the word that I used to describe this was staggering... We're going from $57,292,671 to $61,666,487. That is $4,373,816... 7.63 percent. This is not sustainable... I question what is want and what is needs. And we cannot continue at this rate... I will not be supporting either budget[].”
Key Decisions
Order 2026-44 (bus purchase) passed unanimously, first reading. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Gary Rairdon.

Budget amendment passed 5–1 (Rairdon opposed). Moved by Brian McCambridge; seconder not stated on the recording. For: Brian McCambridge, Michael Shaughnessy, Anna Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham, Jennifer Munro. Against: Gary Rairdon.

Order 2026-45 (FY27 budget, as amended) passed first reading, 5–1 (Rairdon opposed). Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Brian McCambridge. For: Brian McCambridge, Michael Shaughnessy, Anna Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham, Jennifer Munro. Against: Gary Rairdon.

Order 2026-46 (School budget warrants, which are separate budget questions approved by the Council and voters) passed first reading [35:00] 5–1 (Rairdon opposed). After the May 4 second reading, the School Budget goes to voters at the June 9, 2026 referendum. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Brian McCambridge. For: Brian McCambridge, Michael Shaughnessy, Anna Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham, Jennifer Munro. Against: Gary Rairdon.

Order 2026-47 (Wastewater budget: $6,779,069 total, including $4,829,623 Portland Water District assessment, with $5,994,765 in sewer revenue; sewer rate up from $7.73 to $8.35 per hundred cubic feet for calendar year 2027) passed first reading [37:53] unanimously, 6–0 — Rairdon supported this item despite opposing the general budget. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Brian McCambridge.

Public Comment (Second): Pedestrian Safety & Budget Pushback

Resident Josh Blanchard raised a pedestrian-crossing safety concern. Mayor Morse raised a similar issue at the Hannaford crossing. This prompted an extended engineering discussion with Director Eric Dudley.

“That pedestrian alert lighting would at least give the driver the sense that somebody pressed the button and somebody was trying to walk across that street... I have a 16-year-old daughter that is tasked with walking to school.”
blocks.cite: Josh Blanchard (70 New Gorham Rd., public comment)

blocks.x: Dudley explained that the William Clark Drive/New Gorham Road and Hannaford crossings are governed by best-practice engineering standards. The standards are those of the Federal Highway Administration, the Institute of Transportation Engineers, and the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials. They are not state mandates as such. These standards currently limit some requested fixes.

A prior grant application to relocate the Hannaford crosswalk (~$250,000) was unsuccessful on competitive scoring. Dudley said he'd explore nighttime “halo” lighting and consider folding a design study for both locations into the Order 2026-49 Sebago Technics contract.
Councilors Turcotte, Shaughnessy, and Munro all voiced personal concern about these crossings as parents/residents of the area.

Resident Ken Fawson raised a neighborhood speeding/traffic-calming request (citing a child struck by a car roughly eight months prior). Fawson also made a pointed budget critique. He compared Westbrook's proposed 7.65% property tax increase against his prior North Carolina home's taxes and state school rankings.
“This budget doesn't pass the [sniff] test... I agree with Mr. Rairdon. You guys really need to sharpen your pencils because I don't think this is going to pass with the citizens.”
Vice President Shaughnessy responded that North Carolina's stronger county-government structure makes direct comparisons difficult.

Resident Steve Pulsoni separately cited an October 2025 Axios report ranking Maine's five-year electricity price increase highest in the nation (67.4%, with 36% in 2024 alone). Pulsoni encouraged the City to pursue solar/LED savings wherever possible.

A resident also read aloud an unrelated email from a state representative. It publicized an April 29 State House rally in support of Legislative Document (LD) 127, a child-welfare bill, unconnected to city business.
Key Decisions
Informational — no votes taken on this public comment.
Closing
Committee Reports & Executive Session
Discussion Summary
No committee report updates. The Council voted to enter executive session, a closed, private session allowed by state law for certain topics.

The vote cited 1 M.R.S. (Maine Revised Statutes) §405(6)(E) (attorney consultation on legal rights, duties, or pending/contemplated litigation). The Mayor, City Administrator, Assistant City Administrator, City Clerk, Interim and Deputy Directors of Economic Development, Project Manager, and legal counsel were invited to attend. The transcript ends there.
Key Decisions
Motion to enter executive session approved by show of hands. None opposed. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Michael Shaughnessy.
Action Items
None.
